CausalChain: Excessive hepatic stress (e.g., ROS accumulation) → Oxidative modification of Keap1 leads to Nrf2 release → p62 is phosphorylated via mTOR/ULK1, enhancing its binding to Keap1 → p62-mediated autophagic degradation of Keap1 results in sustained Nrf2 activation → Prolonged, unregulated Nrf2 activation promotes metabolic reprogramming that can favor tumorigenesis → Precise modulation of p62 phosphorylation can achieve transient, protective Nrf2 activation without triggering pro-tumorigenic pathways
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that targeted modulation of p62 phosphorylation status, achieved through controlled mTOR/ULK1 signaling, can fine-tune the duration and amplitude of Keap1 degradation and Nrf2 activation in liver cells. Such precise control is expected to confer robust protection against oxidative stress and liver injury (e.g., in NAFLD or viral hepatitis) while avoiding the chronic overactivation of Nrf2 that predisposes to hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Recent studies have underscored the critical role of the Keap1‐Nrf2 pathway in modulating oxidative stress and the progression of various liver diseases. In particular, the interplay between Nrf2 activation and autophagy, governed by the selective degradation of Keap1 via p62, has emerged as a double‐edged sword. While transient activation of Nrf2 confers cytoprotection and detoxification in models of fatty liver disease, viral hepatitis and drug‐induced liver injury, prolonged or unregulated activation may contribute to metabolic reprogramming and hepatocellular carcinoma. Here, we propose a novel hypothesis in which precise modulation of p62 phosphorylation—a process regulated by mTOR and ULK1—can recalibrate the balance between Keap1 degradation and Nrf2 activation. This strategy has the potential to maintain antioxidant defenses and mitigate hepatic injury while minimizing the oncogenic risks associated with chronic Nrf2 overactivation.
